p: A few Western witnesses, including the Latin Bible, read 'the eleven', which fits the story after Judas but not Paul's creed.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (KJV); the great majority of Greek manuscripts
Codex Claromontanus (D, 500s), Old Latin copies and the Latin Vulgate (undecim), as reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus

why: "The Twelve" is the reading of nearly all Greek manuscripts and of every critical edition. "The eleven" is a Western reading (the Greek-Latin copy and the Latin Bible) and looks like a scribe's correction: after Judas, only eleven remained (Luke 24:33; Acts 1:26). Paul uses "the Twelve" as the name of a group, whatever its exact count on a given day. A Catholic reader will find "eleven" in the Vulgate, but that wording reflects the Western Latin copies, not Paul's Greek.
b: Paul's creed gives titles of groups (the Twelve, the apostles). A title can stay when a number changes; Acts 1:15-26 shows the group was refilled to twelve.

a: the grace of God that is with me
t: 'The grace of God that is with me' or 'the grace of God with me'
p: A small article, present in some editions and not in others, changes how 'with me' hangs on the sentence.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text
readings.orig: ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ σὺν ἐμοί
readings.en: the grace of God that is with me
readings.plain: the grace of God that is with me

readings.w: Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.orig: ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ σὺν ἐμοί
readings.en: the grace of God with me
readings.plain: the grace of God with me

why: The article makes "with me" a description of the grace: "the grace of God that is with me." Without it the phrase can be read as "God's grace, together with me." Both readings keep the Greek syn, "with," on which the Catholic and Orthodox contrast with the Reformed rests (see the note), so the article shifts the emphasis a little and does not decide between the churches. The Plain follows the editions that print it.

t: Baptized for them, or for the dead?
p: The oldest editions end the verse 'for them'; the Textus Receptus repeats 'for the dead'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (the manuscripts behind each edition are given in the NA28 apparatus and are not listed here)
Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text

why: "For them" is the harder reading and the shorter; "for the dead" looks like a copyist repeating the phrase from the first half of the verse to make the sense plain. The meaning does not change.

p: The address 'brothers' stands in some editions of this oath and not in others.

readings.w: NA28 and Tyndale House
SBLGNT, the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The meaning is the same either way. The Plain keeps "brothers" because NA28 and Tyndale House print it and Paul often adds the address when he presses a point (15:50, 15:58). The KJV does not have it. The manuscripts on each side are in the NA28 apparatus and are not listed here.

a: If there is such a thing as a natural body, there is a spiritual one too.
t: 'If there is a natural body' or 'There is a natural body'
p: The KJV reads this as two plain statements; the oldest editions read it as 'If ... then'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.orig: εἰ ἔστιν σῶμα ψυχικόν, ἔστιν καὶ πνευματικόν
readings.en: If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual one
readings.plain: If there is such a thing as a natural body, there is a spiritual one too.

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text
readings.orig: ἔστιν σῶμα ψυχικόν, καὶ ἔστιν σῶμα πνευματικόν
readings.en: There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body
readings.plain: There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.

why: The critical text has the "If" and the shorter ending; the Byzantine form states both bodies as facts and repeats "body." The argument is the same: the existence of the natural body is the ground for the spiritual one.

t: 'The second man is from heaven' or 'the Lord from heaven'
p: The KJV reads 'the Lord from heaven'; the older manuscripts do not have 'the Lord'.

readings.w: P46 (about AD 200), Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Ephraemi and several others, as reported by Metzger; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House

Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV); some later correctors and early writers. Metzger reports that the longer wording may come from a text used by Marcion; Tertullian argues against Marcion on this verse in Against Marcion 5.10

why: The shorter reading has the best and oldest witnesses. "The Lord" looks like an addition to make the contrast with Adam explicit. Paul's argument does not depend on it: the "second man" is already Christ.

p: One Greek letter separates a promise ('we will wear') from an exhortation ('let us wear').

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Textus Receptus (KJV); Codex Vaticanus and a few others, as reported by Metzger
Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text; P46, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and many others, as reported by Metzger (the full list is in the NA28 apparatus)

why: The subjunctive has wide and early support, and Tyndale House follows it. The NA28 and SBL editors prefer the future, because "let us wear" would be a sudden exhortation in the middle of a statement about the future (Metzger notes the committee knew the external support favored the subjunctive). The letters omicron and omega were pronounced almost alike in later Greek, so a scribe could write either by ear. The Plain follows the future; the exhortation is not far from Paul's mind in any case.
b: The English difference is small, but it is one of the best-known textual puzzles in the chapter: does Paul promise that believers will bear Christ's image, or urge them to take it up now?

a: not all of us will sleep, but all of us will be changed
t: Who sleeps and who is changed?
p: Early copies and the Latin Bible differ on where the 'not' falls in this famous line. The first three readings give the same meaning.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
readings.orig: πάντες οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα
readings.en: we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed
readings.plain: not all of us will sleep, but all of us will be changed

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV), which add a particle (men, "indeed") after the first "all" without changing the sense
readings.orig: πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα
readings.en: we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed
readings.plain: not all of us will sleep, but all of us will be changed

readings.w: A group of early Alexandrian witnesses reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus, with "not" placed before "all": the order most English readers know
readings.orig: οὐ πάντες κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα
readings.en: not all of us will sleep, but we will all be changed
readings.plain: not all of us will sleep, but all of us will be changed

readings.w: Other early Greek witnesses reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus, which turn the second half around. Jerome (Letter 119) says the Greek copies he knew read "we shall all sleep"
readings.orig: πάντες κοιμηθησόμεθα, οὐ πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα
readings.en: we will all sleep, but not all will be changed
readings.plain: all of us will sleep, but not all of us will be changed

readings.w: Latin Vulgate. This is a Latin reading only; the Greek that lies behind it is not printed here
readings.orig: omnes quidem resurgemus, non omnes immutabimur
readings.en: we will all rise, but not all will be changed
readings.plain: all of us will rise, but not all of us will be changed

why: The first reading has the best combined support among the editors and fits the context: Paul has just said that the living and the dead alike must be changed (verses 50 and 52). The Byzantine particle and the Alexandrian order, "not all of us will sleep," give the same meaning, so the English is the same for all three. The last two readings say that not everyone is changed, which goes against verse 52, "we ourselves will be changed." They probably arose from the worry that Paul had expected to be alive at Christ's return and some of those who heard him had already died. Jerome mentions the difference between the Latin and the Greek in his Letter 119.
b: Metzger, Textual Commentary, sets out these and further forms. The oldest Greek copy of the chapter is P46 (about AD 200).

a: this thing that decays has put on what cannot decay
p: Westcott-Hort print a shorter verse; no English Bible shows the difference.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text
readings.orig: τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσηται ἀφθαρσίαν καὶ
readings.en: this perishable puts on the imperishable, and
readings.plain: this thing that decays has put on what cannot decay

readings.w: Westcott-Hort (shorter text)

why: The longer text has the wider support among the editions. A scribe's eye may have jumped from the first "puts on" to the second, which would give the shorter form. Either way the meaning is the same, since verse 53 has already said both.

a: Death, where is your victory? Death, where is your sting?
p: The KJV says 'O grave'; the older manuscripts say 'Death' twice and put 'victory' first.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (the manuscripts are given in the NA28 apparatus and are not listed here)
readings.orig: ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ νῖκος; ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ κέντρον;
readings.en: Where, Death, is your victory? Where, Death, is your sting?
readings.plain: Death, where is your victory? Death, where is your sting?

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV, "O grave") and the Byzantine text
readings.orig: ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ κέντρον; ποῦ σου, ᾅδη, τὸ νῖκος;
readings.en: Where, Death, is your sting? Where, Hades, is your victory?
readings.plain: Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?

why: The older text repeats "Death" and keeps the order victory then sting, which matches the order of the quotations in verse 54. The Byzantine text seems to have borrowed "Hades" from the Greek of Hosea 13:14 and swapped the two clauses. Both readings mean the same thing: the final defeat of the power of death.

p: Paul uses the short form 'Prisca'; later copies and the KJV use 'Priscilla', as Acts does.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (manuscripts as in the NA28 apparatus)
Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text, matching Acts

why: Paul uses "Prisca" in every letter in which he names her. Copyists changed it to "Priscilla" (the form in Acts) to make the letters agree. Both are the same woman.

t: One word or two? Maran atha
p: The Aramaic can be split two ways, giving a prayer ('come') or a statement ('has come').

readings.w: SBLGNT and NA28 (marana tha, "Our Lord, come")
Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text (maran atha, "Our Lord has come" or "is coming"), and the form in the KJV

why: The early manuscripts were written without breaks between words, so the choice was made later by editors. The Greek of Revelation 22:20, "Come, Lord Jesus," supports the prayer, and the Didache (10:6) closes its eucharistic prayers with the same Aramaic words. The division marana tha is the one most scholars favor, but maran atha was the usual reading in the Latin and Greek churches.

p: The KJV adds 'Jesus Christ' to the curse; the older manuscripts do not.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (manuscripts as in the NA28 apparatus)
Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text

why: The shorter reading has the better evidence, and the longer one is the sort of expansion copyists often made in sacred titles.

t: 'The Lord Jesus' or 'the Lord Jesus Christ'
p: The final blessing is longer in the KJV, which adds 'Christ'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles (manuscripts as in the NA28 apparatus)
Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text

why: The shorter blessing is the older. "Christ" was added in later copies, a common lengthening of the name.

p: Some copies add 'Amen' and a note saying the letter was sent from Philippi; the note cannot be right.

readings.w: SBLGNT and NA28 (no "Amen"); Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Tyndale House, Textus Receptus (KJV) and the Byzantine text (add "Amen"); the Textus Receptus also adds a postscript

why: A closing "Amen" was a common liturgical addition by copyists. The Textus Receptus goes further and adds a scribal postscript: "The first letter to the Corinthians was written from Philippi through Stephanas, Fortunatus, Achaicus and Timothy." Such postscripts come from late scribes and are not part of the letter. This one is plainly wrong, because 16:8 puts Paul in Ephesus, and Philippi is not mentioned anywhere in the letter.
